papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: An Effective Strategy for Deep Learning Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: The increasing size and complexity of deep learning models present significant challenges for deployment in real-world, resource-constrained environments. Model compression techniques have emerged as a critical field of study to address these issues. Knowledge distillation, a prominent compression method, involves training a smaller 'student' model to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. This process transfers the rich, nuanced knowledge learned by the teacher, enabling the student model to achieve performance far exceeding what it could attain by training on ground-truth labels alone. This approach has proven versatile, with applications spanning natural language processing, computer vision, and recommender systems, leading to models that are not only smaller and faster but also maintain high levels of accuracy, facilitating the practical application of state-of-the-art deep learning.

papers_seen.author: Taylor
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Versatile Technique for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a powerful and flexible technique for model compression within deep learning. This process operates on a teacher-student framework, where a smaller, more efficient 'student' model is trained to mimic the behavior and replicate the performance of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. The primary goal is to reduce the computational and memory footprint of complex neural networks, making them suitable for deployment in resource-constrained environments such as mobile devices. Beyond simple compression, research has shown that knowledge distillation can also enhance the performance of student models. Its applications are broad, spanning critical domains like natural language processing and computer vision, demonstrating its importance in making advanced AI systems more practical and accessible.

papers_seen.author: Whitehead
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression and Performance Enhancement
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful technique in deep learning for model compression and performance improvement. This process involves training a smaller, more efficient 'student' model to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. Traditionally, this is achieved by using the teacher's softened output probabilities as supervisory signals for the student. However, recent advancements have explored mimicking intermediate feature representations, which can provide richer information. The applications of knowledge distillation are diverse, extending to compressing large language models, improving low-precision networks, and enabling collaborative training in privacy-sensitive settings like federated learning. Furthermore, research challenges the conventional view of a superior teacher guiding a weaker student, suggesting that the regularization effect of the process is a key component of its success, even leading to teacher-free distillation frameworks.

papers_seen.author: Young
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Technique for Model Compression and Performance Enhancement
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a prominent technique in deep learning for transferring knowledge from a large, complex 'teacher' model to a smaller, more efficient 'student' model. This process serves a dual purpose: it facilitates model compression, enabling the deployment of state-of-the-art models on resource-constrained devices, and it often enhances the performance and generalization capabilities of the student model beyond what could be achieved through standard training. Its applications are broad, spanning natural language processing, computer vision, and recommender systems, proving to be a flexible and powerful tool for optimizing deep neural networks for practical use.

papers_seen.author: Zavala
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Model Compression and Beyond
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a crucial technique in deep learning for model compression. This process operates on a teacher-student paradigm, where a smaller, more efficient 'student' model is trained to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. The primary objective is to create compact models suitable for deployment on resource-constrained devices without a significant loss in performance. By transferring the rich, nuanced information captured by the teacher, such as output probabilities and intermediate feature representations, the student model can achieve high accuracy. The utility of knowledge distillation extends beyond simple compression, serving as a powerful framework for enhancing model performance, improving generalization, and transferring complex capabilities across diverse domains like natural language processing and computer vision.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Model Compression and Enhancement
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a prominent model compression technique in deep learning that facilitates the creation of compact, efficient student models by transferring knowledge from larger, more complex teacher models. This teacher-student learning paradigm enables the deployment of powerful neural networks in resource-constrained environments, such as on mobile devices, without a significant loss in performance. The process typically involves training the student to mimic the outputs or internal representations of the teacher. Beyond its primary application in creating lightweight models, knowledge distillation has evolved into a versatile framework used to enhance model generalization, transfer knowledge across different architectures, and enable advanced learning strategies.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Framework for Model Compression and Enhancement
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained models have demonstrated state-of-the-art performance but are often too large and slow for practical deployment. Knowledge distillation addresses this by training a smaller, more efficient 'student' model to mimic the behavior of a larger 'teacher' model. This process transfers the rich, generalized knowledge from the teacher, enabling the student to achieve comparable performance with a fraction of the computational resources. The technique has been adapted into various forms, including self-distillation where a model learns from its own past predictions and multi-teacher frameworks that leverage knowledge from an ensemble of models. Knowledge distillation is broadly applied across domains like natural language processing and computer vision to not only compress models but also to improve their interpretability, robustness, and performance on specialized tasks.

papers_seen.author: Ross
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Model Compression and Enhancement
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a prominent model compression technique in deep learning that addresses the challenge of deploying large, complex models in resource-constrained environments. The process involves a teacher-student paradigm, where a smaller, more efficient 'student' model is trained to mimic the behavior and performance of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. This knowledge transfer allows the student to achieve high accuracy without the computational overhead of the teacher. The versatility of this framework has led to its successful application across numerous domains, including natural language processing and computer vision, making it a critical tool for developing practical and accessible artificial intelligence systems.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Technique for Model Compression and Beyond
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a popular model compression technique in deep learning that facilitates the deployment of large, complex models in resource-constrained environments. The core idea involves transferring knowledge from a large, pre-trained 'teacher' model to a smaller 'student' model, enabling the student to achieve comparable performance with significantly fewer parameters and lower computational cost. Beyond simple compression, this paradigm has been adapted to address a wide range of challenges. Researchers have successfully employed knowledge distillation to enhance model fairness by mitigating algorithmic and gender biases, to improve data privacy by creating models with differential privacy guarantees, and even to develop student models that outperform their teachers. This adaptability across various domains, including natural language processing and graph-based learning, highlights knowledge distillation as a powerful and flexible tool in the development of efficient and responsible AI systems.

papers_seen.author: Novak
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Technique for Model Compression and Enhancement
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful paradigm in deep learning where a compact student model is trained to reproduce the behavior of a larger, more complex teacher model. Originally conceived for model compression, this technique enables the deployment of powerful neural networks on resource-constrained devices by creating smaller, faster versions without a significant loss in performance. Beyond compression, knowledge distillation has proven to be a versatile framework with applications in domain adaptation, lifelong learning, privacy preservation, and improving the generalization capabilities of models. By transferring nuanced knowledge from the teacher, such as class relationship probabilities and internal feature representations, the student model can often achieve better performance and robustness than if it were trained on ground-truth labels alone.

papers_seen.author: Shaw
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression and Performance Enhancement
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful technique in deep learning for model compression and knowledge transfer. The core concept involves training a smaller, more efficient "student" model to replicate the performance of a larger, pre-trained "teacher" model. This process allows for the deployment of complex neural networks on resource-constrained devices by creating lightweight versions without a significant drop in accuracy. Beyond compression, knowledge distillation is also used to enhance model performance, transfer capabilities across different model architectures or data modalities, and address challenges such as privacy in federated learning and adversarial robustness. Its applications are widespread, spanning natural language processing, computer vision, speech recognition, and graph-based learning.

papers_seen.author: Lee
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Framework for Model Compression and Enhancement
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a model compression paradigm where a smaller 'student' model is trained to mimic the behavior of a larger, more powerful 'teacher' model. This process enables the deployment of complex deep learning architectures in resource-constrained environments by reducing their computational and memory footprints. The core principle involves transferring the generalized knowledge from the teacher to the student, often using the teacher's output probabilities as soft labels. The applications of this technique have expanded beyond simple compression to include enhancing model performance, improving robustness, and enabling novel learning scenarios like data-free training and federated learning across heterogeneous devices.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers with Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of unifying knowledge from a set of classifiers with different architectures and target classes into a single classifier, given only a generic set of unlabelled data. We call this problem Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers (UHC). This problem is motivated by scenarios where data is collected from multiple sources, but the sources cannot share their data, e.g., due to privacy concerns, and only privately trained models can be shared. In addition, each source may not be able to gather data to train all classes due to data availability at each source, and may not be able to train the same classification model due to different computational resources. To tackle this problem, we propose a generalisation of knowledge distillation to merge HCs. We derive a probabilistic relation between the outputs of HCs and the probability over all classes. Based on this relation, we propose two classes of methods based on cross-entropy minimisation and matrix factorisation, which allow us to estimate soft labels over all classes from unlabelled samples and use them in lieu of ground truth labels to train a unified classifier. Our extensive experiments on ImageNet, LSUN, and Places365 datasets show that our approaches significantly outperform a naive extension of distillation and can achieve almost the same accuracy as classifiers that are trained in a centralised, supervised manner.

papers_seen.author: Chandler
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Framework for Model Compression and Knowledge Transfer
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a model compression paradigm in deep learning designed to create smaller, more efficient models from larger, more complex ones. This technique operates on a teacher-student framework, where a compact student model is trained to replicate the behavior and performance of a larger, pre-trained teacher model. The primary goal is to enable the deployment of powerful deep learning architectures in resource-constrained environments, such as mobile or edge devices. This process allows the student to inherit the rich knowledge learned by the teacher, resulting in a lightweight model that retains high performance. The applications of knowledge distillation are diverse, extending beyond simple compression to areas like domain adaptation, federated learning, and improving model interpretability.

papers_seen.author: House
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Model Compression and Knowledge Transfer
papers_seen.abstract: Deep learning models, particularly large-scale language models, have achieved state-of-the-art performance but their immense size and computational requirements hinder their deployment in resource-constrained environments. Knowledge distillation has emerged as a powerful model compression technique to address this challenge. This method involves training a smaller, more efficient 'student' model to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. The applications of knowledge distillation are diverse, extending beyond simple compression to enable complex distributed learning paradigms like federated learning on heterogeneous devices. Advanced methods leverage multiple teachers to improve knowledge transfer, and innovative approaches even permit distillation without access to the original training data. Furthermore, the technique can be adapted to various model architectures, including generative networks, and can be used to improve the interpretability of complex deep neural networks.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Large-scale deep learning models have achieved state-of-the-art performance in numerous fields, but their significant computational and memory requirements hinder their deployment on resource-constrained devices. Knowledge distillation has emerged as a prominent model compression technique to address this challenge. This method involves training a smaller, more efficient "student" model to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained "teacher" model. By transferring the rich knowledge learned by the teacher, the student model can achieve comparable performance while being significantly smaller and faster. This approach has been successfully applied across various domains, including natural language processing and computer vision, with specialized techniques developed for challenges such as domain adaptation, cross-modal learning, and scenarios where original training data is unavailable.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: The Versatility of Knowledge Distillation for Efficient and Robust Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful model compression technique where a smaller "student" model learns from a larger "teacher" model. This process enables the deployment of complex neural networks on resource-constrained devices. Beyond simple size reduction, distillation can transfer inductive biases, improve performance on downstream tasks, and enhance model efficiency across various domains like natural language processing, computer vision, and graph learning. The framework is highly adaptable, extending to scenarios involving ensemble models, self-improvement, and addressing broader concerns such as data privacy and algorithmic fairness, making it a cornerstone of modern machine learning engineering.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Cross-modal Knowledge Distillation for Vision-to-Sensor Action Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: Human activity recognition (HAR) based on multi-modal approach has been recently shown to improve the accuracy performance of HAR. However, restricted computational resources associated with wearable devices, i.e., smartwatch, failed to directly support such advanced methods. To tackle this issue, this study introduces an end-to-end Vision-to-Sensor Knowledge Distillation (VSKD) framework. In this VSKD framework, only time-series data, i.e., accelerometer data, is needed from wearable devices during the testing phase. Therefore, this framework will not only reduce the computational demands on edge devices, but also produce a learning model that closely matches the performance of the computational expensive multi-modal approach. In order to retain the local temporal relationship and facilitate visual deep learning models, we first convert time-series data to two-dimensional images by applying the Gramian Angular Field ( GAF) based encoding method. We adopted ResNet18 and multi-scale TRN with BN-Inception as teacher and student network in this study, respectively. A novel loss function, named Distance and Angle-wised Semantic Knowledge loss (DASK), is proposed to mitigate the modality variations between the vision and the sensor domain. Extensive experimental results on UTD-MHAD, MMAct, and Berkeley-MHAD datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and competitiveness of the proposed VSKD model which can deployed on wearable sensors.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Deep learning models, particularly in fields like natural language processing, have grown significantly in size and computational cost, posing challenges for deployment on resource-constrained devices. Model compression aims to create smaller, more efficient models while retaining high performance. Knowledge distillation is a prominent compression paradigm where a compact 'student' model is trained to mimic the behavior of a larger 'teacher' model. This approach transfers the learned knowledge of the teacher, enabling the smaller student to achieve better performance than if trained alone. Knowledge distillation has been successfully applied across various domains, with research exploring advanced techniques such as transferring knowledge from intermediate layers, using multiple teachers, and performing distillation without access to the original training data.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Model Compression and Knowledge Transfer
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful training paradigm where a smaller "student" model learns from a larger, pre-trained "teacher" model. Initially conceived for model compression, this technique enables the development of lightweight, efficient neural networks that retain the high performance of their cumbersome counterparts. Beyond creating faster and smaller models, the applications of knowledge distillation have expanded significantly. It is now a crucial tool for a range of tasks including domain adaptation, where models must adjust to new data distributions, and federated learning, which facilitates collaborative training across distributed devices with heterogeneous models without sharing private data. The success of distillation often depends on sophisticated strategies that go beyond simple output matching, such as aligning intermediate feature representations and leveraging statistically sound data augmentation. Despite its power, challenges in optimization remain, but knowledge distillation continues to be a versatile and impactful framework in modern deep learning.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Releasing Graph Neural Networks with Differential Privacy Guarantees
papers_seen.abstract: With the increasing popularity of graph neural networks (GNNs) in several sensitive applications like healthcare and medicine, concerns have been raised over the privacy aspects of trained GNNs. More notably, GNNs are vulnerable to privacy attacks, such as membership inference attacks, even if only black-box access to the trained model is granted. We propose PrivGNN, a privacy-preserving framework for releasing GNN models in a centralized setting. Assuming an access to a public unlabeled graph, PrivGNN provides a framework to release GNN models trained explicitly on public data along with knowledge obtained from the private data in a privacy preserving manner. PrivGNN combines the knowledge-distillation framework with the two noise mechanisms, random subsampling, and noisy labeling, to ensure rigorous privacy guarantees. We theoretically analyze our approach in the Renyi differential privacy framework. Besides, we show the solid experimental performance of our method compared to several baselines adapted for graph-structured data. Our code is available at https://github.com/iyempissy/privGnn.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Unified Visual Transformer Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Vision transformers (ViTs) have gained popularity recently. Even without customized image operators such as convolutions, ViTs can yield competitive performance when properly trained on massive data. However, the computational overhead of ViTs remains prohibitive, due to stacking multi-head self-attention modules and else. Compared to the vast literature and prevailing success in compressing convolutional neural networks, the study of Vision Transformer compression has also just emerged, and existing works focused on one or two aspects of compression. This paper proposes a unified ViT compression framework that seamlessly assembles three effective techniques: pruning, layer skipping, and knowledge distillation. We formulate a budget-constrained, end-to-end optimization framework, targeting jointly learning model weights, layer-wise pruning ratios/masks, and skip configurations, under a distillation loss. The optimization problem is then solved using the primal-dual algorithm. Experiments are conducted with several ViT variants, e.g. DeiT and T2T-ViT backbones on the ImageNet dataset, and our approach consistently outperforms recent competitors. For example, DeiT-Tiny can be trimmed down to 50\% of the original FLOPs almost without losing accuracy. Codes are available online:~\url{https://github.com/VITA-Group/UVC}.

papers_seen.author: Owens
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Paradigm for Efficient and Adaptable Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a prominent technique in deep learning for compressing large, complex models into smaller, more efficient counterparts. This process, where a compact "student" model learns from a larger "teacher" model, is crucial for deploying state-of-the-art neural networks on resource-constrained devices. Beyond simple compression, distillation has evolved into a versatile framework for transferring knowledge in a variety of challenging contexts. It enables training without access to original data, facilitates collaborative learning across heterogeneous devices in federated settings, and improves model generalization and adaptation to new domains. This demonstrates that knowledge distillation is not merely a compression tool but a fundamental paradigm for making advanced artificial intelligence more practical, private, and widely applicable.

papers_seen.author: Daniels
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Model Compression Technique in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Deep learning models have demonstrated state-of-the-art performance across many fields, but their large size and high computational requirements often hinder their deployment in real-world, resource-constrained environments. Model compression techniques aim to address this challenge by creating smaller, faster, and more efficient models. Knowledge distillation is a prominent compression paradigm that involves transferring knowledge from a large, pre-trained 'teacher' model to a more compact 'student' model. This process allows the student model to achieve performance comparable to the teacher while having a significantly smaller footprint. The applications of knowledge distillation are diverse, spanning natural language processing, computer vision, and recommender systems. Advanced methods have been developed to handle various scenarios, including using multiple teachers, transferring knowledge across different data modalities, and applying distillation in distributed learning frameworks. These techniques are crucial for enabling the practical use of powerful deep learning models in production systems.

papers_seen.author: Cortez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Model Compression in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a critical and powerful technique for model compression within the field of deep learning. This paradigm addresses the challenge of deploying large, computationally intensive models in resource-constrained environments by transferring knowledge from a large 'teacher' model to a smaller, more efficient 'student' model. The student is trained to mimic the behavior of the teacher, often by learning from its softened probability outputs or intermediate feature representations. This process allows the compact student model to achieve high performance, often comparable to its much larger teacher, without the associated computational and memory overhead. The versatility of this framework is demonstrated by its successful application across numerous domains, including natural language processing and computer vision, making it an essential tool for developing practical and deployable AI systems.

papers_seen.author: Young
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Deep Learning Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a powerful and flexible technique for compressing large deep learning models. This method involves training a smaller, computationally efficient 'student' model to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. By transferring the nuanced 'dark knowledge' from the teacher's predictions, rather than just learning from ground-truth labels, the student model can achieve performance comparable to its larger counterpart while being significantly smaller and faster. This approach has proven effective across a wide range of applications, including natural language processing, computer vision, and federated learning, enabling the deployment of state-of-the-art models on resource-constrained devices without a substantial sacrifice in accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Henson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Model Compression and Enhancement
papers_seen.abstract: As deep learning models increase in size and complexity, their deployment in real-world, resource-constrained applications has become a significant challenge. Model compression techniques aim to create smaller, faster, and more efficient models without substantial performance degradation. Among these techniques, knowledge distillation has emerged as a particularly powerful and flexible paradigm. It employs a teacher-student framework where a compact student model is trained to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained teacher model, thereby inheriting its learned knowledge. While its primary application is to reduce model size for environments with limited computational resources, the utility of knowledge distillation extends further. This technique has been shown to improve model performance, enhance interpretability, and facilitate knowledge transfer across different domains and architectures, making it an indispensable tool in modern deep learning.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Versatile Framework for Model Compression and Knowledge Transfer
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a prominent technique in deep learning for compressing large, complex models into smaller, more efficient counterparts. The process involves a compact 'student' model learning to mimic the behavior of a larger 'teacher' model, enabling the deployment of powerful neural networks on resource-constrained devices. Knowledge is typically transferred by having the student replicate the teacher's output probabilities or its internal feature representations. This methodology has been successfully applied across numerous domains, including natural language processing and computer vision. Beyond simple compression, knowledge distillation has evolved into a versatile framework that can enhance model generalization, facilitate domain adaptation, and enable collaborative learning in settings like federated learning, making advanced artificial intelligence more practical and widely accessible.

papers_seen.author: Rice
papers_seen.title: CoReD: Generalizing Fake Media Detection with Continual Representation using Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Over the last few decades, artificial intelligence research has made tremendous strides, but it still heavily relies on fixed datasets in stationary environments. Continual learning is a growing field of research that examines how AI systems can learn sequentially from a continuous stream of linked data in the same way that biological systems do. Simultaneously, fake media such as deepfakes and synthetic face images have emerged as significant to current multimedia technologies. Recently, numerous method has been proposed which can detect deepfakes with high accuracy. However, they suffer significantly due to their reliance on fixed datasets in limited evaluation settings. Therefore, in this work, we apply continuous learning to neural networks' learning dynamics, emphasizing its potential to increase data efficiency significantly. We propose Continual Representation using Distillation (CoReD) method that employs the concept of Continual Learning (CL), Representation Learning (RL), and Knowledge Distillation (KD). We design CoReD to perform sequential domain adaptation tasks on new deepfake and GAN-generated synthetic face datasets, while effectively minimizing the catastrophic forgetting in a teacher-student model setting. Our extensive experimental results demonstrate that our method is efficient at domain adaptation to detect low-quality deepfakes videos and GAN-generated images from several datasets, outperforming the-state-of-art baseline methods.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Understanding BERT Rankers Under Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep language models such as BERT pre-trained on large corpus have given a huge performance boost to the state-of-the-art information retrieval ranking systems. Knowledge embedded in such models allows them to pick up complex matching signals between passages and queries. However, the high computation cost during inference limits their deployment in real-world search scenarios. In this paper, we study if and how the knowledge for search within BERT can be transferred to a smaller ranker through distillation. Our experiments demonstrate that it is crucial to use a proper distillation procedure, which produces up to nine times speedup while preserving the state-of-the-art performance.

papers_seen.author: Rhodes
papers_seen.title: Lifelong Language Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: It is challenging to perform lifelong language learning (LLL) on a stream of different tasks without any performance degradation comparing to the multi-task counterparts. To address this issue, we present Lifelong Language Knowledge Distillation (L2KD), a simple but efficient method that can be easily applied to existing LLL architectures in order to mitigate the degradation. Specifically, when the LLL model is trained on a new task, we assign a teacher model to first learn the new task, and pass the knowledge to the LLL model via knowledge distillation. Therefore, the LLL model can better adapt to the new task while keeping the previously learned knowledge. Experiments show that the proposed L2KD consistently improves previous state-of-the-art models, and the degradation comparing to multi-task models in LLL tasks is well mitigated for both sequence generation and text classification tasks.

papers_seen.author: Gaines
papers_seen.title: AdaBERT: Task-Adaptive BERT Compression with Differentiable Neural Architecture Search
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained language models such as BERT have shown their effectiveness in various natural language processing tasks. However, the huge parameter size makes them difficult to be deployed in real-time applications that require quick inference with limited resources. Existing methods compress BERT into small models while such compression is task-independent, i.e., the same compressed BERT for all different downstream tasks. Motivated by the necessity and benefits of task-oriented BERT compression, we propose a novel compression method, AdaBERT, that leverages differentiable Neural Architecture Search to automatically compress BERT into task-adaptive small models for specific tasks. We incorporate a task-oriented knowledge distillation loss to provide search hints and an efficiency-aware loss as search constraints, which enables a good trade-off between efficiency and effectiveness for task-adaptive BERT compression. We evaluate AdaBERT on several NLP tasks, and the results demonstrate that those task-adaptive compressed models are 12.7x to 29.3x faster than BERT in inference time and 11.5x to 17.0x smaller in terms of parameter size, while comparable performance is maintained.

papers_seen.author: Yu
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Deep Learning Model Compression and Enhancement
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful model compression paradigm where a compact 'student' model learns from a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. This technique aims to create smaller, more efficient networks that retain the high performance of their cumbersome counterparts, making them suitable for deployment on resource-constrained devices. Initially focused on mimicking output probabilities, the field has evolved to encompass a wide range of applications beyond simple classification, including complex tasks in natural language processing and computer vision. The effectiveness of distillation is now understood to hinge on more sophisticated methods, such as transferring knowledge from internal feature representations and adapting the process to transfer specific qualities like adversarial robustness. Modern approaches integrate distillation with other compression techniques and advanced training strategies, demonstrating its versatility and importance in developing state-of-the-art, deployable deep learning models.

papers_seen.author: Torres
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Deep Learning Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful model compression technique in deep learning that enables the deployment of large, complex models in resource-constrained environments. The method involves training a compact 'student' model to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. This process transfers the rich, nuanced knowledge from the teacher, allowing the student to achieve comparable performance with significantly fewer computational resources. By reducing model size and inference time, knowledge distillation facilitates the practical application of state-of-the-art architectures across diverse domains, including natural language processing and computer vision, making advanced artificial intelligence more accessible and efficient.

papers_seen.author: Bowman
papers_seen.title: TRILLsson: Distilled Universal Paralinguistic Speech Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Recent advances in self-supervision have dramatically improved the quality of speech representations. However, deployment of state-of-the-art embedding models on devices has been restricted due to their limited public availability and large resource footprint. Our work addresses these issues by publicly releasing a collection of paralinguistic speech models that are small and near state-of-the-art performance. Our approach is based on knowledge distillation, and our models are distilled on public data only. We explore different architectures and thoroughly evaluate our models on the Non-Semantic Speech (NOSS) benchmark. Our largest distilled model is less than 15% the size of the original model (314MB vs 2.2GB), achieves over 96% the accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks, and is trained on 6.5% the data. The smallest model is 1% in size (22MB) and achieves over 90% the accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks. Our models outperform the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 model on 6 of 7 tasks, and our smallest model outperforms the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 on both emotion recognition tasks despite being 7% the size.

papers_seen.author: Cobb
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Framework for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a model compression paradigm designed to create efficient, lightweight deep learning models. It operates on a teacher-student framework, where a smaller "student" model is trained to mimic the behavior and knowledge of a larger, more powerful "teacher" model. The primary goal is to reduce the computational and memory footprint of state-of-the-art networks, enabling their deployment in resource-constrained environments such as mobile devices. Methodologies for knowledge transfer have evolved from matching output probabilities to more advanced techniques that focus on intermediate feature representations. This versatile technique has been successfully applied across numerous domains, including computer vision, natural language processing, and graph-based learning, demonstrating its effectiveness beyond simple compression to enhance overall model performance.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Channel Distillation: Channel-Wise Attention for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is to transfer the knowledge from the data learned by the teacher network to the student network, so that the student has the advantage of less parameters and less calculations, and the accuracy is close to the teacher. In this paper, we propose a new distillation method, which contains two transfer distillation strategies and a loss decay strategy. The first transfer strategy is based on channel-wise attention, called Channel Distillation (CD). CD transfers the channel information from the teacher to the student. The second is Guided Knowledge Distillation (GKD). Unlike Knowledge Distillation (KD), which allows the student to mimic each sample's prediction distribution of the teacher, GKD only enables the student to mimic the correct output of the teacher. The last part is Early Decay Teacher (EDT). During the training process, we gradually decay the weight of the distillation loss. The purpose is to enable the student to gradually control the optimization rather than the teacher. Our proposed method is evaluated on ImageNet and CIFAR100. On ImageNet, we achieve 27.68% of top-1 error with ResNet18, which outperforms state-of-the-art methods. On CIFAR100, we achieve surprising result that the student outperforms the teacher. Code is available at https://github.com/zhouzaida/channel-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: BERT Learns to Teach: Knowledge Distillation with Meta Learning
papers_seen.abstract: We present Knowledge Distillation with Meta Learning (MetaDistil), a simple yet effective alternative to traditional knowledge distillation (KD) methods where the teacher model is fixed during training. We show the teacher network can learn to better transfer knowledge to the student network (i.e., learning to teach) with the feedback from the performance of the distilled student network in a meta learning framework. Moreover, we introduce a pilot update mechanism to improve the alignment between the inner-learner and meta-learner in meta learning algorithms that focus on an improved inner-learner. Experiments on various benchmarks show that MetaDistil can yield significant improvements compared with traditional KD algorithms and is less sensitive to the choice of different student capacity and hyperparameters, facilitating the use of KD on different tasks and models.

papers_seen.author: Richards
papers_seen.title: TextKD-GAN: Text Generation using KnowledgeDistillation and Generative Adversarial Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Text generation is of particular interest in many NLP applications such as machine translation, language modeling, and text summarization. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) achieved a remarkable success in high quality image generation in computer vision,and recently, GANs have gained lots of interest from the NLP community as well. However, achieving similar success in NLP would be more challenging due to the discrete nature of text. In this work, we introduce a method using knowledge distillation to effectively exploit GAN setup for text generation. We demonstrate how autoencoders (AEs) can be used for providing a continuous representation of sentences, which is a smooth representation that assign non-zero probabilities to more than one word. We distill this representation to train the generator to synthesize similar smooth representations. We perform a number of experiments to validate our idea using different datasets and show that our proposed approach yields better performance in terms of the BLEU score and Jensen-Shannon distance (JSD) measure compared to traditional GAN-based text generation approaches without pre-training.

papers_seen.author: Cannon
papers_seen.title: Model Compression and Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a prominent technique for model compression, enabling the deployment of large, complex deep learning models on resource-constrained devices. This process typically involves a teacher-student framework, where a smaller student model learns to mimic the behavior and performance of a larger, pre-trained teacher model. This paradigm addresses the significant computational and storage costs associated with state-of-the-art models in fields like Natural Language Processing and computer vision. Various methods have been developed to tackle challenges such as data privacy, architectural mismatches between teacher and student, and information transfer efficiency. Applications are diverse, ranging from compressing large language models and generative adversarial networks to enhancing model robustness against adversarial attacks and enabling efficient federated learning. Extensions to the basic framework include using multiple teachers, adversarial learning, and data-free distillation techniques, continually expanding the utility of this compression strategy.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: DINE: Domain Adaptation from Single and Multiple Black-box Predictors
papers_seen.abstract: To ease the burden of labeling, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) aims to transfer knowledge in previous and related labeled datasets (sources) to a new unlabeled dataset (target). Despite impressive progress, prior methods always need to access the raw source data and develop data-dependent alignment approaches to recognize the target samples in a transductive learning manner, which may raise privacy concerns from source individuals. Several recent studies resort to an alternative solution by exploiting the well-trained white-box model from the source domain, yet, it may still leak the raw data through generative adversarial learning. This paper studies a practical and interesting setting for UDA, where only black-box source models (i.e., only network predictions are available) are provided during adaptation in the target domain. To solve this problem, we propose a new two-step knowledge adaptation framework called DIstill and fine-tuNE (DINE). Taking into consideration the target data structure, DINE first distills the knowledge from the source predictor to a customized target model, then fine-tunes the distilled model to further fit the target domain. Besides, neural networks are not required to be identical across domains in DINE, even allowing effective adaptation on a low-resource device. Empirical results on three UDA scenarios (i.e., single-source, multi-source, and partial-set) confirm that DINE achieves highly competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art data-dependent approaches. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/tim-learn/DINE/}.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a prominent model compression technique used to transfer knowledge from a large, complex 'teacher' model to a smaller, more efficient 'student' model. This process enables the deployment of powerful deep learning architectures in resource-constrained environments, such as mobile devices, without a significant loss in performance. The core idea involves training the student not only on the ground-truth data but also using the outputs or intermediate representations of the trained teacher as a richer, soft target. This method has been successfully applied across numerous domains, including natural language processing, computer vision, speech recognition, and recommender systems, leading to a wide range of lightweight models that retain the capabilities of their larger counterparts.

papers_seen.author: Stewart
papers_seen.title: Private Model Compression via Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The soaring demand for intelligent mobile applications calls for deploying powerful deep neural networks (DNNs) on mobile devices. However, the outstanding performance of DNNs notoriously relies on increasingly complex models, which in turn is associated with an increase in computational expense far surpassing mobile devices' capacity. What is worse, app service providers need to collect and utilize a large volume of users' data, which contain sensitive information, to build the sophisticated DNN models. Directly deploying these models on public mobile devices presents prohibitive privacy risk. To benefit from the on-device deep learning without the capacity and privacy concerns, we design a private model compression framework RONA. Following the knowledge distillation paradigm, we jointly use hint learning, distillation learning, and self learning to train a compact and fast neural network. The knowledge distilled from the cumbersome model is adaptively bounded and carefully perturbed to enforce differential privacy. We further propose an elegant query sample selection method to reduce the number of queries and control the privacy loss. A series of empirical evaluations as well as the implementation on an Android mobile device show that RONA can not only compress cumbersome models efficiently but also provide a strong privacy guarantee. For example, on SVHN, when a meaningful $(9.83,10^{-6})$-differential privacy is guaranteed, the compact model trained by RONA can obtain 20$\times$ compression ratio and 19$\times$ speed-up with merely 0.97% accuracy loss.

papers_seen.author: Higgins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: An Effective Technique for Model Compression in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: As deep learning models grow in size and complexity, their deployment in resource-constrained environments becomes a significant challenge. Model compression techniques are essential for creating smaller, faster, and more efficient models without substantial performance degradation. Knowledge distillation has emerged as a powerful paradigm for this purpose. It involves transferring knowledge from a large, cumbersome 'teacher' model to a smaller 'student' model. The student learns to mimic the rich output distributions of the teacher, thereby inheriting its performance capabilities while maintaining a much smaller footprint. This approach has proven effective across various domains, including natural language processing and computer vision, enabling the use of state-of-the-art architectures in practical, real-world applications.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a prominent technique in deep learning for model compression, where a compact "student" model is trained to mimic the behavior of a larger, more complex "teacher" model. This process facilitates the deployment of state-of-the-art neural networks in resource-constrained environments, such as mobile devices, by significantly reducing their size and computational requirements. Beyond compression, knowledge distillation has evolved into a versatile framework capable of enhancing model performance, improving generalization, and enabling novel applications across various domains. By transferring the rich, nuanced knowledge learned by the teacher, student models can achieve higher accuracy and robustness than they could by training on ground-truth labels alone.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Wide Neural Networks: Risk Bound, Data Efficiency and Imperfect Teacher
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a strategy of training a student network with guide of the soft output from a teacher network. It has been a successful method of model compression and knowledge transfer. However, currently knowledge distillation lacks a convincing theoretical understanding. On the other hand, recent finding on neural tangent kernel enables us to approximate a wide neural network with a linear model of the network's random features. In this paper, we theoretically analyze the knowledge distillation of a wide neural network. First we provide a transfer risk bound for the linearized model of the network. Then we propose a metric of the task's training difficulty, called data inefficiency. Based on this metric, we show that for a perfect teacher, a high ratio of teacher's soft labels can be beneficial. Finally, for the case of imperfect teacher, we find that hard labels can correct teacher's wrong prediction, which explains the practice of mixing hard and soft labels.

papers_seen.author: Daniel
papers_seen.title: Data-Free Adversarial Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) has made remarkable progress in the last few years and become a popular paradigm for model compression and knowledge transfer. However, almost all existing KD algorithms are data-driven, i.e., relying on a large amount of original training data or alternative data, which is usually unavailable in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we devote ourselves to this challenging problem and propose a novel adversarial distillation mechanism to craft a compact student model without any real-world data. We introduce a model discrepancy to quantificationally measure the difference between student and teacher models and construct an optimizable upper bound. In our work, the student and the teacher jointly act the role of the discriminator to reduce this discrepancy, when a generator adversarially produces some "hard samples" to enlarge it. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed data-free method yields comparable performance to existing data-driven methods. More strikingly, our approach can be directly extended to semantic segmentation, which is more complicated than classification, and our approach achieves state-of-the-art results. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/VainF/Data-Free-Adversarial-Distillation.

papers_seen.author: Evans

papers_seen.author: Taylor
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Versatile Technique for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a powerful and flexible technique for model compression within deep learning. This process operates on a teacher-student framework, where a smaller, more efficient 'student' model is trained to mimic the behavior and replicate the performance of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. The primary goal is to reduce the computational and memory footprint of complex neural networks, making them suitable for deployment in resource-constrained environments such as mobile devices. Beyond simple compression, research has shown that knowledge distillation can also enhance the performance of student models. Its applications are broad, spanning critical domains like natural language processing and computer vision, demonstrating its importance in making advanced AI systems more practical and accessible.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: Improved Feature Distillation via Projector Ensemble
papers_seen.abstract: In knowledge distillation, previous feature distillation methods mainly focus on the design of loss functions and the selection of the distilled layers, while the effect of the feature projector between the student and the teacher remains under-explored. In this paper, we first discuss a plausible mechanism of the projector with empirical evidence and then propose a new feature distillation method based on a projector ensemble for further performance improvement. We observe that the student network benefits from a projector even if the feature dimensions of the student and the teacher are the same. Training a student backbone without a projector can be considered as a multi-task learning process, namely achieving discriminative feature extraction for classification and feature matching between the student and the teacher for distillation at the same time. We hypothesize and empirically verify that without a projector, the student network tends to overfit the teacher's feature distributions despite having different architecture and weights initialization. This leads to degradation on the quality of the student's deep features that are eventually used in classification. Adding a projector, on the other hand, disentangles the two learning tasks and helps the student network to focus better on the main feature extraction task while still being able to utilize teacher features as a guidance through the projector. Motivated by the positive effect of the projector in feature distillation, we propose an ensemble of projectors to further improve the quality of student features. Experimental results on different datasets with a series of teacher-student pairs illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: A Deep Hierarchical Approach to Lifelong Learning in Minecraft
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a lifelong learning system that has the ability to reuse and transfer knowledge from one task to another while efficiently retaining the previously learned knowledge-base. Knowledge is transferred by learning reusable skills to solve tasks in Minecraft, a popular video game which is an unsolved and high-dimensional lifelong learning problem. These reusable skills, which we refer to as Deep Skill Networks, are then incorporated into our novel Hierarchical Deep Reinforcement Learning Network (H-DRLN) architecture using two techniques: (1) a deep skill array and (2) skill distillation, our novel variation of policy distillation (Rusu et. al. 2015) for learning skills. Skill distillation enables the HDRLN to efficiently retain knowledge and therefore scale in lifelong learning, by accumulating knowledge and encapsulating multiple reusable skills into a single distilled network. The H-DRLN exhibits superior performance and lower learning sample complexity compared to the regular Deep Q Network (Mnih et. al. 2015) in sub-domains of Minecraft.

papers_seen.author: Fletcher
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a critical technique for model compression in deep learning. This approach facilitates the transfer of knowledge from a large, complex model, known as the teacher, to a smaller, more computationally efficient student model. The primary goal is to create compact models that retain the high performance of their larger counterparts, making them suitable for deployment in resource-constrained environments. The process often involves transferring knowledge from the teacher's output distributions and intermediate features, not just the final predictions. This versatile framework has been successfully applied across various domains, including natural language processing and computer vision. Advanced strategies such as multi-teacher distillation, self-distillation, and teacher-free distillation have further expanded its utility, demonstrating its importance in developing practical and efficient AI systems.

papers_seen.author: Abbott
papers_seen.title: Compressing Deep Graph Neural Networks via Adversarial Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep graph neural networks (GNNs) have been shown to be expressive for modeling graph-structured data. Nevertheless, the over-stacked architecture of deep graph models makes it difficult to deploy and rapidly test on mobile or embedded systems. To compress over-stacked GNNs, knowledge distillation via a teacher-student architecture turns out to be an effective technique, where the key step is to measure the discrepancy between teacher and student networks with predefined distance functions. However, using the same distance for graphs of various structures may be unfit, and the optimal distance formulation is hard to determine. To tackle these problems, we propose a novel Adversarial Knowledge Distillation framework for graph models named GraphAKD, which adversarially trains a discriminator and a generator to adaptively detect and decrease the discrepancy. Specifically, noticing that the well-captured inter-node and inter-class correlations favor the success of deep GNNs, we propose to criticize the inherited knowledge from node-level and class-level views with a trainable discriminator. The discriminator distinguishes between teacher knowledge and what the student inherits, while the student GNN works as a generator and aims to fool the discriminator. To our best knowledge, GraphAKD is the first to introduce adversarial training to knowledge distillation in graph domains. Experiments on node-level and graph-level classification benchmarks demonstrate that GraphAKD improves the student performance by a large margin. The results imply that GraphAKD can precisely transfer knowledge from a complicated teacher GNN to a compact student GNN.

papers_seen.author: Conner
papers_seen.title: Distilling Task-Specific Knowledge from BERT into Simple Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: In the natural language processing literature, neural networks are becoming increasingly deeper and complex. The recent poster child of this trend is the deep language representation model, which includes BERT, ELMo, and GPT. These developments have led to the conviction that previous-generation, shallower neural networks for language understanding are obsolete. In this paper, however, we demonstrate that rudimentary, lightweight neural networks can still be made competitive without architecture changes, external training data, or additional input features. We propose to distill knowledge from BERT, a state-of-the-art language representation model, into a single-layer BiLSTM, as well as its siamese counterpart for sentence-pair tasks. Across multiple datasets in paraphrasing, natural language inference, and sentiment classification, we achieve comparable results with ELMo, while using roughly 100 times fewer parameters and 15 times less inference time.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Understanding BERT Rankers Under Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep language models such as BERT pre-trained on large corpus have given a huge performance boost to the state-of-the-art information retrieval ranking systems. Knowledge embedded in such models allows them to pick up complex matching signals between passages and queries. However, the high computation cost during inference limits their deployment in real-world search scenarios. In this paper, we study if and how the knowledge for search within BERT can be transferred to a smaller ranker through distillation. Our experiments demonstrate that it is crucial to use a proper distillation procedure, which produces up to nine times speedup while preserving the state-of-the-art performance.

papers_seen.author: Beck
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile and Effective Framework for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Modern deep learning models often have immense computational requirements, limiting their use in practical applications. Knowledge distillation offers a powerful solution for model compression. This technique involves training a compact 'student' model to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. papers_seen.author: Jordan

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful technique in deep learning where knowledge from a large, complex "teacher" model is transferred to a smaller, more efficient "student" model. Originally conceived as a method for model compression, its applications have expanded significantly. This technique not only enables the deployment of state-of-the-art models in resource-constrained environments but also serves as a mechanism to enhance the performance of student models beyond what they could achieve through standard training. The versatility of knowledge distillation is demonstrated by its application across diverse domains, from natural language processing to computer vision. Recent advancements have introduced more dynamic and effective distillation frameworks, such as online and self-distillation, and have even leveraged the technique to improve model interpretability.

papers_seen.author: Lawrence
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge From a Deep Pose Regressor Network
papers_seen.abstract: This paper presents a novel method to distill knowledge from a deep pose regressor network for efficient Visual Odometry (VO). Standard distillation relies on "dark knowledge" for successful knowledge transfer. As this knowledge is not available in pose regression and the teacher prediction is not always accurate, we propose to emphasize the knowledge transfer only when we trust the teacher. We achieve this by using teacher loss as a confidence score which places variable relative importance on the teacher prediction. We inject this confidence score to the main training task via Attentive Imitation Loss (AIL) and when learning the intermediate representation of the teacher through Attentive Hint Training (AHT) approach. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work which successfully distill the knowledge from a deep pose regression network. Our evaluation on the KITTI and Malaga dataset shows that we can keep the student prediction close to the teacher with up to 92.95% parameter reduction and 2.12x faster in computation time.

papers_seen.author: Ross
papers_seen.title: Ensemble Distillation for Neural Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation describes a method for training a student network to perform better by learning from a stronger teacher network. Translating a sentence with an Neural Machine Translation (NMT) engine is time expensive and having a smaller model speeds up this process. We demonstrate how to transfer the translation quality of an ensemble and an oracle BLEU teacher network into a single NMT system. Further, we present translation improvements from a teacher network that has the same architecture and dimensions of the student network. As the training of the student model is still expensive, we introduce a data filtering method based on the knowledge of the teacher model that not only speeds up the training, but also leads to better translation quality. Our techniques need no code change and can be easily reproduced with any NMT architecture to speed up the decoding process.

papers_seen.author: Aguirre

Model compression techniques aim to address this challenge by creating smaller, more efficient models. Knowledge distillation has emerged as a prominent and versatile framework for this purpose. This technique operates on a teacher-student paradigm, where a compact 'student' model is trained to mimic the behavior and replicate the knowledge of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. The goal is to produce a lightweight model that retains the high performance of its larger counterpart, making it suitable for deployment in resource-constrained environments like mobile devices. This approach has proven effective across a wide range of applications, including computer vision and natural language processing.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Less is More: Task-aware Layer-wise Distillation for Language Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Layer-wise distillation is a powerful tool to compress large models (i.e. teacher models) into small ones (i.e., student models). The student distills knowledge from the teacher by mimicking the hidden representations of the teacher at every intermediate layer. However, layer-wise distillation is difficult. Since the student has a smaller model capacity than the teacher, it is often under-fitted. Furthermore, the hidden representations of the teacher contain redundant information that the student does not necessarily need for the target task's learning. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Task-aware layEr-wise Distillation (TED). TED designs task-aware filters to align the hidden representations of the student and the teacher at each layer. The filters select the knowledge that is useful for the target task from the hidden representations. As such, TED reduces the knowledge gap between the two models and helps the student to fit better on the target task. We evaluate TED in two scenarios: continual pre-training and fine-tuning. TED demonstrates significant and consistent improvements over existing distillation methods in both scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/cliang1453/task-aware-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Model Compression and Enhancement
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has become a pivotal technique in deep learning for compressing large, complex models into smaller, more efficient versions. This process involves a teacher-student framework where a compact student model is trained to mimic the behavior and performance of a larger teacher model. The primary benefit is enabling the deployment of state-of-the-art models in resource-constrained environments, such as mobile devices, where computational power and memory are limited. The applications of this technique are widespread, spanning natural language processing and computer vision. Beyond simple model size reduction, knowledge distillation is also used to enhance a model's performance, transfer beneficial properties between architectures, and improve generalization.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Compressing GANs using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been used in several machine learning tasks such as domain transfer, super resolution, and synthetic data generation. State-of-the-art GANs often use tens of millions of parameters, making them expensive to deploy for applications in low SWAP (size, weight, and power) hardware, such as mobile devices, and for applications with real time capabilities. There has been no work found to reduce the number of parameters used in GANs. Therefore, we propose a method to compress GANs using knowledge distillation techniques, in which a smaller "student" GAN learns to mimic a larger "teacher" GAN. We show that the distillation methods used on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Celeb-A datasets can compress teacher GANs at ratios of 1669:1, 58:1, and 87:1, respectively, while retaining the quality of the generated image. From our experiments, we observe a qualitative limit for GAN's compression. Moreover, we observe that, with a fixed parameter budget, compressed GANs outperform GANs trained using standard training methods. We conjecture that this is partially owing to the optimization landscape of over-parameterized GANs which allows efficient training using alternating gradient descent. Thus, training an over-parameterized GAN followed by our proposed compression scheme provides a high quality generative model with a small number of parameters.

papers_seen.author: House
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Model Compression and Knowledge Transfer
papers_seen.abstract: Deep learning models, particularly large-scale language models, have achieved state-of-the-art performance but their immense size and computational requirements hinder their deployment in resource-constrained environments. Knowledge distillation has emerged as a powerful model compression technique to address this challenge. This method involves training a smaller, more efficient 'student' model to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. The applications of knowledge distillation are diverse, extending beyond simple compression to enable complex distributed learning paradigms like federated learning on heterogeneous devices. Advanced methods leverage multiple teachers to improve knowledge transfer, and innovative approaches even permit distillation without access to the original training data. Furthermore, the technique can be adapted to various model architectures, including generative networks, and can be used to improve the interpretability of complex deep neural networks.

papers_seen.author: Powers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Technique for Model Compression and Performance Enhancement
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful machine learning technique for compressing large, complex models into smaller, more efficient versions without a significant loss in performance. This process involves training a smaller 'student' model to replicate the behavior of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. The core idea is to transfer the generalized knowledge learned by the teacher, which is often encoded in its output probabilities, to the student. This allows for the deployment of state-of-the-art models in resource-constrained environments, such as mobile devices or applications with strict latency requirements. The applications of knowledge distillation are broad, spanning natural language processing, computer vision, recommender systems, and graph-based learning. Beyond simple model compression, distillation has been shown to improve the accuracy of student models, facilitate domain adaptation, and enable training even when the original data is unavailable.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Releasing Graph Neural Networks with Differential Privacy Guarantees
papers_seen.abstract: With the increasing popularity of graph neural networks (GNNs) in several sensitive applications like healthcare and medicine, concerns have been raised over the privacy aspects of trained GNNs. More notably, GNNs are vulnerable to privacy attacks, such as membership inference attacks, even if only black-box access to the trained model is granted. We propose PrivGNN, a privacy-preserving framework for releasing GNN models in a centralized setting. Assuming an access to a public unlabeled graph, PrivGNN provides a framework to release GNN models trained explicitly on public data along with knowledge obtained from the private data in a privacy preserving manner. PrivGNN combines the knowledge-distillation framework with the two noise mechanisms, random subsampling, and noisy labeling, to ensure rigorous privacy guarantees. We theoretically analyze our approach in the Renyi differential privacy framework. Besides, we show the solid experimental performance of our method compared to several baselines adapted for graph-structured data. Our code is available at https://github.com/iyempissy/privGnn.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a popular model compression paradigm in deep learning. It operates on a teacher-student framework, where a compact student model is trained to replicate the performance of a larger, more complex teacher model. This process enables the deployment of powerful models on resource-constrained devices, which is critical for many real-world applications. The applications of knowledge distillation are diverse, spanning natural language processing tasks like language model compression and computer vision tasks such as compressing generative models. Researchers have developed numerous variations of the core technique, including methods that leverage multiple teachers, distill knowledge from intermediate network layers, and perform distillation without access to the original training data. Beyond creating smaller and faster models, knowledge distillation is also used to achieve other objectives, such as enhancing model privacy, improving interpretability, and mitigating biases.

papers_seen.author: Cohen
papers_seen.title: ALP-KD: Attention-Based Layer Projection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is considered as a training and compression strategy in which two neural networks, namely a teacher and a student, are coupled together during training. The teacher network is supposed to be a trustworthy predictor and the student tries to mimic its predictions. Usually, a student with a lighter architecture is selected so we can achieve compression and yet deliver high-quality results. In such a setting, distillation only happens for final predictions whereas the student could also benefit from teacher's supervision for internal components.   Motivated by this, we studied the problem of distillation for intermediate layers. Since there might not be a one-to-one alignment between student and teacher layers, existing techniques skip some teacher layers and only distill from a subset of them. This shortcoming directly impacts quality, so we instead propose a combinatorial technique which relies on attention. Our model fuses teacher-side information and takes each layer's significance into consideration, then performs distillation between combined teacher layers and those of the student. Using our technique, we distilled a 12-layer BERT (Devlin et al. 2019) into 6-, 4-, and 2-layer counterparts and evaluated them on GLUE tasks (Wang et al. 2018). Experimental results show that our combinatorial approach is able to outperform other existing techniques.
